question: Fruit of the Spirit. How do you know it's the Spirit and not just you?
intro: You get a feeling in church. Peace, maybe. Or a nudge to call someone. Was that the Holy Ghost, or was that you being tired and sentimental? People say "I felt the Spirit" about everything from a testimony to a sunset. Paul gives a list of what the Spirit produces. It's more specific than a warm feeling. This week is about learning to tell the difference, because if you can't, you'll either trust everything or nothing.

days.q: What does the Spirit produce?
days.intro: Read Galatians 5. Paul contrasts two lists: what the flesh produces and what the Spirit produces. When you read, notice the second list isn't feelings. It's character. Love, joy, peace, patience. Things you'd see in a person over time, not in a moment.
days.journal: When was the last time you were sure you felt the Spirit? What was it like, specifically? Write it down.

days.q: Why "fruit" and not "fruits"?
days.intro: In the Greek it's singular. One fruit, nine flavors. Paul's saying the Spirit produces one thing in you, a kind of person, and love, joy, peace, and the rest are what that person looks like. Contrast "works of the flesh," plural, which is a pile of separate acts. Read the lists again with that in mind. Then read Jesus on how you tell a good tree.
days.journal: If the Spirit produces a kind of person, not a feeling, does that change how you'd answer "do I have the Spirit"?

days.q: What does the Restoration say about recognizing Him?
days.intro: The Lord had to teach Oliver Cowdery this exact thing. Twice. Read the two revelations, then the one to Hyrum, which has the simplest test in scripture: does it lead you to do good? Then Moroni, who says everything good comes from God and you can judge it as plainly as day from night.
days.journal: D&C 11:12 says trust the Spirit that leads to do good. Think of the feeling from Day 1. Did it lead you to do good? What?

days.q: What does an apostle say about keeping the Spirit close?
days.intro: President Henry B. Eyring, October 2015. He describes what having the Holy Ghost as a companion actually feels like day to day.

read.talk: The Holy Ghost as Your Companion
read.speaker: Henry B. Eyring

days.takeaway: His point is that the Spirit's presence is quieter than people expect and it's mostly noticed in what you *want*. When He's with you, you want to be kinder, you want to pray, you want to forgive. Eyring says you can tell He's been with you more by looking back at your day than by checking for a feeling in the moment. And you get more of Him by acting on the small promptings you already got.
days.journal: Eyring says look back at your day to see where He was. Do it now. Where was He today?

days.q: But sincere people feel confirmed about opposite things. So what's the feeling worth?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. Two people pray about the same decision and feel peace about different answers. Somebody in another religion feels the same burning you do. So is the feeling evidence of anything? Read John's instruction to *test* the spirits. Read the Lord on how gifts get distributed. Then decide what a feeling proves and what it doesn't.
days.journal: If someone from another faith told you they felt the Spirit, what would you say? What does that mean about your own feelings?

days.q: How do you get better at telling?
days.intro: The Nephites at Bountiful heard a voice from heaven three times before they understood it. The first two times they didn't. Practice matters. The Lord says sanctify yourself and your mind gets single to Him, and then you see. When you read, look for what makes the difference between hearing and understanding.
read: Preach My Gospel, chapter 4, "Recognize the Spirit" and the list of how the Spirit communicates
days.journal: Pick one flavor of the fruit from Galatians 5:22-23. Watch for it this week, in yourself and others. Write down one time you saw it and whether you think it was the Spirit.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Galatians 5. Read the list one more time. Then read your Day 1 answer and Day 4 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: How do you know it's the Spirit and not just you? Give yourself a real test, not a slogan.

question: Why does the Church need apostles and prophets?
intro: Paul says the Church is built on the foundation of apostles and prophets. Not on a book. Not on individual inspiration. On people, called and sent. Most of Christianity says that ended with the Bible. We say it didn't, and it's one of the main reasons we exist. But have you actually thought about *why* God does it that way? What does a prophet give you that scripture and the Spirit don't? This week is that question.

days.q: What did Paul say the Church is built on?
days.intro: Read Ephesians 2, where Paul describes the foundation. Then Ephesians 4, where he lists what apostles and prophets are *for* and how long they're needed. When you read chapter 4, find the answer to "until when." It's specific.
days.journal: Ephesians 4 says apostles are needed until we all come to unity of the faith. Are we there yet? What would you say to someone who says they ended with the Bible?

days.q: What is an apostle, actually?
days.intro: Greek: *apostolos*, one who is sent. Not a title. A job. Jesus picked twelve on purpose, matching the twelve tribes, and when Judas died they filled the seat. The office was meant to continue. Read Him praying all night before He picked them, then the replacement of Judas, then Amos, who said God does nothing without telling a prophet first.
read: Luke 6:12-13 (He prayed all night before choosing them)
days.journal: Jesus prayed all night before calling the Twelve. What decision in your life deserved a whole night of prayer and didn't get one?

days.q: What does the Restoration say the office is for?
days.intro: The Lord defines the job in D&C 107: special witnesses of Christ, in all the world. Then read Him telling the Saints that His voice and His servants' voice are the same. Then read the Nephite version, where Jesus picks twelve on this continent too.
days.journal: D&C 1:38 says the Lord's word by His servants is the same as by Him. Do you actually treat conference like that? What's the gap?

days.q: What does an apostle say about being one?
days.intro: Elder David A. Bednar, October 2015. He describes what happened when he was called, what he was told his job was, and what he saw the other apostles do.

read.talk: Chosen to Bear Testimony of My Name
read.speaker: David A. Bednar

days.takeaway: His point is that the apostles' one job is to be witnesses of Christ. Everything else is downstream of that. He describes watching the senior apostles, some of them old and sick, keep testifying anyway, and says their witness is what holds the Church together. He also says something people miss: the apostles are ordinary men who were called, not extraordinary men who were found.
days.journal: Bednar says apostles are ordinary men, called. Does that make their witness weaker or stronger to you?

days.q: If I have the Spirit, why do I need a middleman?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. You can pray. You can get revelation. So why does God route things through fifteen men in Salt Lake? Isn't that exactly the kind of priestcraft the Book of Mormon warns about? Read the Lord telling Oliver Cowdery who gets revelation for the Church and who doesn't. Read Hebrews on authority. Then read Nephi on what actual priestcraft looks like, and see whether it matches.
days.journal: D&C 28 says one person gets revelation for the whole Church. Why do you think God does it that way instead of everyone hearing directly?

days.q: How do you actually follow a prophet?
days.intro: Sustaining isn't a vote. The Lord says receive his word in patience and faith, and that the gates of hell won't prevail against you if you do. Isaiah describes how beautiful the feet of the one who brings good news are, and Abinadi says that's every prophet. When you read, look for what the promise is attached to. It's not agreement. It's something else.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 1, "Apostles and Prophets" and "The Restoration of the Gospel through Joseph Smith"
days.journal: Pick the most recent thing the prophet asked. Not your favorite. The most recent. Are you doing it? Write yes or no and why.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Ephesians 4. Read the "until" verses one more time. Then read your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question the way you'd say it to a Christian friend: Why does the Church need apostles and prophets now?

question: "I can do all things through Christ." Really? All things?
intro: It's on posters, t-shirts, and the back of athletes' cleats. "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me." But Paul wrote it from prison. He didn't get out. He was eventually executed. So he clearly didn't mean "I can do anything I set my mind to." What did he mean? This week is about the verse people quote most and understand least, and what strength through Christ actually looks like when things don't work out.

days.q: What did Paul say, and what was around it?
days.intro: Read the whole passage, not the one line. Paul is talking about being content whether he's full or hungry, rich or broke. *That's* the "all things." He's not promising success. He's describing a man who can't be knocked over. When you read, list what he says he's learned.
days.journal: What's the "all things" you've been hoping this verse covers? Write it down. We'll see if Paul meant that.

days.q: Where was he when he wrote it?
days.intro: Prison. Probably Rome, chained to a guard. He'd been shipwrecked, beaten, stoned, and left for dead. The Greek word for "content" is *autarkes*, self-sufficient, though Paul flips it to Christ-sufficient. "Strengtheneth" is *endunamoo*, to be made strong from the inside. Read what Paul said about being in prison, and his line about living and dying. Then you'll know what kind of strength he meant.
days.journal: Paul in chains says his imprisonment helped the gospel spread. What's the thing in your life that feels like chains? What would it look like to see it his way?

days.q: Who in the Book of Mormon said the same thing?
days.intro: Ammon. Almost word for word. "In his strength I can do all things." And Ammon had the receipts: he'd just spent fourteen years doing things that shouldn't have worked. Read his boast, which he's careful to say is in God, not himself. Then Nephi on the ship and Alma's people under burdens. When you read, look at what the strength was *for* in each case.
days.journal: Ammon says he can do all things in God's strength. What's the thing he actually did with it? Was it what he'd have picked?

days.q: What does the prophet say about drawing on that power?
days.intro: President Russell M. Nelson, April 2017. He asked a room full of people whether they were actually accessing the Savior's power or just talking about it.

read.talk: Drawing the Power of Jesus Christ into Our Lives
read.speaker: Russell M. Nelson

days.takeaway: His point is that the Savior's power is real, available, and mostly unused. He says most of us have no idea how much He's willing to do for us because we don't ask in the right way. Nelson's method: study the Atonement seriously, use the Topical Guide, learn everything you can about what Christ actually did, and then reach for that power on purpose. It's not automatic. You have to draw it.
days.journal: Nelson says the power is available and mostly unused. What's one thing you've been trying to do in your own strength that you could actually ask Him to strengthen you in?

days.q: What about when it doesn't work?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. Paul was strengthened and still got executed. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego said God could save them "but if not" they still wouldn't bow. Hebrews 11 lists people who got miracles and then, in the same breath, people who didn't. So what does "I can do all things" mean when the thing you're praying for doesn't happen? Read these and decide whether the verse is about outcomes or about something else.
read: Alma 14:11 (Alma unable to save the believers)
days.journal: "But if not." Take your "all things" from Day 1. Can you say "but if not" about it? What would that cost you?

days.q: How do you actually draw on it?
days.intro: Isaiah says the ones who wait on the Lord get their strength renewed. Not the ones who push harder. The Lord tells His missionaries He'll be on their right hand and left. Paul's own answer is that the strength shows up in weakness, not around it. When you read, look for the posture. It's more like leaning than lifting.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 2, "The Atonement" (the section on how it strengthens us)
days.journal: Pick one hard thing this week. Before you do it, pray specifically for His strength in *that* thing. Then write down what happened, even if it's "nothing I could tell."

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Philippians 4. Read verses 11 through 13 one more time, all three. Then read your Day 1 and Day 5 answers.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: What did Paul mean by "I can do all things through Christ"? And what does it mean for the thing you wrote on Day 1?

question: "Fight the good fight." What was Paul actually fighting?
intro: Paul's last letter, written while he waited to be executed, has one of the best lines in scripture: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Preach My Gospel calls this enduring to the end, the fifth principle of the gospel. It's the one nobody teaches well. It sounds like gritting your teeth until you die. Paul didn't sound like he was gritting anything. So what was the fight, and how do you fight it without being miserable?

days.q: What did Paul say at the end?
days.intro: Read the end of 2 Timothy. Paul knows he's about to die. He's not scared. Read what he says about it, and then go back to the beginning of the letter where he tells Timothy not to be ashamed. When you read, notice he uses three images: a fight, a race, and a trust. Different things.
days.journal: Paul says he's kept the faith. What does "keeping" faith look like for you, day to day? Not gaining it. Keeping it.

days.q: What was the fight?
days.intro: The Greek word is *agon*, where we get "agony." It's an athletic contest, a wrestling match, a race. Paul used sports language constantly. Read him describing the race in Corinthians, and the writer of Hebrews describing it with a stadium full of people watching. The fight wasn't against Rome. It was against quitting.
days.journal: Paul's fight was against giving up, not against an enemy. What's the thing you're most tempted to quit on right now? Church? A calling? A person?

days.q: What does the Book of Mormon call it?
days.intro: Nephi has the clearest description of enduring anywhere: press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, a perfect brightness of hope, and love. That's not gritting teeth. Read him. Then read the resurrected Christ giving the same instruction, and the Lord's shortest version of it in the D&C.
days.journal: Nephi says press forward with brightness of hope. Is your endurance bright, or is it just endurance? What's the difference?

days.q: What does an apostle say about not quitting?
days.intro: President Henry B. Eyring, October 2018. The title is the whole talk, and he means it.
days.takeaway: His point is that discipleship is mostly getting back up. He doesn't promise it gets easy. He says the Lord's expectation is that you keep trying, and that trying *is* the faith, not a warmup for it. He tells stories about people who failed and kept going, and says that's what the Lord counts. The only real failure is quitting, and even that can be undone.
days.journal: Eyring says trying is the faith. What have you stopped trying at because you failed? Is it too late to try again?

days.q: Is enduring supposed to be joyless?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. "Endure to the end" sounds like a sentence, not a promise. And some people who endured for decades quit near the end. Oliver Cowdery left. Martin Harris left. Both came back, but they left. Read the moment the disciples abandoned Jesus and Peter's answer for why he stayed. Read Jesus on looking back. Then read Ammon, who endured plenty and was anything but joyless.
days.journal: Peter said "to whom shall we go?" Is that why you stay? Is that a good enough reason? What's a better one?

days.q: How do you actually keep going?
days.intro: This week connects to Week 4 and Week 11. Read what you wrote when you redefined "perfect" and "repent." Enduring is just those two things repeated: getting more complete, turning again. Then read Alma's counsel to his son, which is the simplest instruction for enduring in scripture: counsel with the Lord in all thy doings.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 3, "Endure to the End"
days.journal: Alma says counsel with the Lord in *all* your doings. Pick one part of your life you've never actually counseled with Him about. Do it tonight. Write what you asked.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Paul in prison. Read 2 Timothy 4:7 one more time. Then read your Day 1 and Day 5 answers.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: What was Paul fighting? And what are you fighting?

question: Paul warned about a falling away. Did it happen?
intro: Paul told the Thessalonians the Second Coming wouldn't happen until there was a "falling away first." He told the Ephesian elders wolves would come after he left. He told Timothy people would stop putting up with sound doctrine. Every one of them was predicting the same thing: the Church would fall apart. We say it did. Most Christians say it didn't, or that the Reformation fixed it. This week is about what Paul saw coming and whether it came.

days.q: What did Paul and the others actually predict?
days.intro: Read Paul's goodbye to the Ephesian elders first. He'd warned them with tears for three years, and when he left they wept because they'd never see him again. Then read his warning to the Thessalonians. When you read, notice he's not vague. He describes what it'll look like.
days.journal: Before this week, what would you have said if a friend asked what "the Great Apostasy" means? Write it down.

days.q: What does "apostasy" mean, and was it foretold earlier?
days.intro: Greek: *apostasia*, a defection, a rebellion, walking away from where you stood. It's the word for a soldier deserting. Amos saw it centuries before Paul: a famine, not of bread, but of hearing the word of the Lord. Isaiah saw the ordinances being changed. Read them. Then read Peter and John describing it already starting while they were alive.
days.journal: Amos calls it a famine of hearing God's word. Have you ever felt that famine personally? What was it like?

days.q: What does the Restoration say happened?
days.intro: Nephi saw the church going into the wilderness, and the Book of Mormon calls the result a church that's "built up" instead of the Lord's. Then read the Lord's own summary in D&C 1, and what He told Joseph Smith in the grove. When you read, look for what was lost. It's not that people stopped being good. It's something more specific.
days.journal: JS-H 1:19 says they had a form of godliness but denied the power. What's the difference between the form and the power? Have you ever had one without the other?

days.q: What does an apostle say about why the Church exists?
days.intro: Elder D. Todd Christofferson, October 2015. A lot of people ask why they need a church at all if they have Jesus. He answers.
days.takeaway: His point is that the Church isn't an optional add-on to personal faith. Christ organized one on purpose, with authority, ordinances, and structure, because some things can't be done alone: you can't baptize yourself, you can't take the sacrament alone, and you can't be a Zion people by yourself. The apostasy wasn't that people stopped believing. It's that the organization Christ built, with its authority, came apart.
days.journal: Christofferson says some things can't be done alone. What's one thing the Church gives you that you literally couldn't get by yourself?

days.q: Were there no good Christians for 1,700 years?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. If the Church fell away, what about all the sincere Christians in between? The monks who copied scripture, the reformers who died for it, your ancestors who prayed? Were they nothing? Read Nephi seeing the Spirit work on Columbus and the reformers. Read Moroni on the light of Christ given to everyone. Read Alma on God speaking to all nations. Then answer carefully.
days.journal: The Restoration says the authority was lost, not the goodness. Does that distinction hold up for you? What would you say to a devout Catholic grandmother about her faith?

days.q: Can it happen to you?
days.intro: Apostasy isn't just a historical event. The word means walking away, and people do it one step at a time. Helaman describes exactly how the Spirit withdraws from a people and it's gradual. The Lord tells Joseph the same thing about individuals. When you read, look for the mechanism. Then read King Benjamin on how to not drift.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 1, "The Great Apostasy"
days.journal: Helaman says the Spirit withdraws when people harden their hearts and it's gradual. Where's one place you've drifted a step without noticing? Write it, then write the step back.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Paul's warning. Read 2 Thessalonians 2 one more time. Then read your Day 1 answer.
days.journal: Answer the week's question the way you'd say it to a friend from another church: Did the falling away happen? And what does that mean for them?

question: Conference week. Which talk from October got under your skin?
intro: Same deal as Week 29. No topic picked ahead of time. You pick one talk from October 2027 general conference, the one that hit hardest or bugged you most, and we take it apart for a week. If you did Week 29, go read what you wrote on Day 7 there first. It'll be interesting to see what you got out of the last one. Then pick your talk and write the speaker and title in your Day 1 journal.

days.q: What did the speaker actually say?
days.intro: Read the whole talk, start to finish. Not the highlights. The talk. When you read, mark the one sentence that stopped you and the one you pushed back on. There's always one of each.
days.journal: Write the speaker and title. Then the sentence that stopped you and the sentence you pushed back on.

days.q: What scriptures did they build it on?
days.intro: List every scripture the speaker cited. Read at least three in context, the verses around them, not just the line. When you read, figure out why the speaker picked *that* verse and not another one.
read: Every scripture cited in your talk (list them)
Three of them, read in context
days.journal: Which scripture was carrying the talk? Did context change what you thought the speaker meant?

days.q: What does the rest of scripture say about it?
days.intro: Find your own. Two scriptures the speaker didn't use, one Book of Mormon and one D&C, that teach the same point. Topical Guide or search bar. You're the student now, not the audience.
read: One Book of Mormon passage on the talk's main point (you find it)
One D&C passage on the same point (you find it)
days.journal: Write the two references you found. Did either say it better than the talk?

days.q: Who else talked about it?
days.intro: Find a second talk from the same conference on a related topic. Read it. Compare. When you read, look for where they agree and where they come at it differently.
read: A second talk from October 2027 on a related topic
days.takeaway: Write your own. Two or three sentences on what the second speaker added.
days.journal: What did the second speaker see that the first one didn't say?

days.q: What did they ask you to do that you don't want to?
days.intro: Every talk has an ask. Find it. If you're happy to do it, it's probably not the real ask. Look harder.
read: Your talk again, just the last third
days.journal: What did the speaker ask you to do? Write the actual ask. Then write why you haven't done it yet.

days.q: Do it.
days.intro: No reading today. Take the ask from Day 5 and do the first step. Today. Then write what happened. If you can't figure out the first step, that's the entry.
days.journal: What did you do? What happened? What's next?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Read your Day 1 entry. Then reread the paragraph with the sentence that stopped you.
read: That one paragraph of your talk
days.journal: Rewrite the talk's main point in your own words, two sentences, like you're telling a friend who didn't watch.

question: Why did Jesus have to "learn obedience by the things which he suffered"?
intro: Hebrews says something about Jesus that should make you stop: He *learned* obedience. Through suffering. If He was already perfect, what was there to learn? And if He had to learn it that way, what does that say about how you learn it? This week is about a Savior who grew, and what His growing means for yours.

days.q: What does Hebrews actually say?
days.intro: Read Hebrews 5, the verses about Jesus praying with strong crying and tears and learning obedience. Then read chapter 2, where the writer says He was made perfect *through* suffering and that's why He can help. When you read, notice how many times the word "suffer" shows up.
days.journal: Jesus learned obedience through suffering. What's something you've learned only by suffering? Write it down.

days.q: What was the writer getting at?
days.intro: Hebrews was written to Jewish Christians who knew the high priest system. Every year the high priest went into the Holy of Holies for the people. The writer says Jesus is the real high priest, and the reason He can do the job is that He's *been* where you are. Read chapter 4, which is the point of the whole book. When you read, look for why His suffering makes Him qualified.
days.journal: Hebrews 4:15 says He was tempted in all points like you, without sin. Which temptation are you most surprised He'd understand?

days.q: What does the Restoration say about how He grew?
days.intro: D&C 93 says something almost nobody teaches: Jesus didn't receive the fulness at first. He got grace for grace, and continued until He did. King Benjamin described what He'd suffer 120 years early. And the Lord told Joseph that the Son had descended below all of it. When you read, look for the word "continued."
days.journal: D&C 93 says He went from grace to grace. If the Son of God had to grow that way, what does that do to your impatience with yourself?

days.q: What does an apostle say about carrying loads?
days.intro: Elder David A. Bednar, April 2014. He tells a story about a truck stuck in the snow and what got it out, and then explains how the Savior's yoke works.

read.talk: Bear Up Their Burdens with Ease
read.speaker: David A. Bednar

days.takeaway: His point is that the load is what gives you traction. The truck couldn't get out of the snow until it was loaded with wood. He says the Savior doesn't always remove the burden, He makes you strong enough that it becomes the thing that moves you forward. And the yoke is shared. You're not pulling alone. You're pulling *with* Him, and He's been under the same yoke.
days.journal: Bednar says the load gives traction. What's the load you've been asking to have removed that might be the thing moving you?

days.q: If He had to learn, was He ever not perfect?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. If Jesus learned obedience, was there a time He didn't have it? Did He ever fail? Luke says He grew in wisdom and stature. The Joseph Smith Translation says He didn't need anyone to teach Him. Hebrews says without sin. So what does "learned" mean for someone who never sinned? Read these and try to hold both: He grew, and He never fell.
read: Joseph Smith Translation, Matthew 3:24-26 (in the appendix)
days.journal: Can you learn something without failing at it first? What would it mean that Jesus did?

days.q: How do you learn obedience from your own suffering?
days.intro: Hebrews 12 says chastening isn't fun while it's happening but it produces something afterward, *if* you let it. Alma says the people who get humble without being forced are more blessed. The Lord told Joseph all of it would give him experience. When you read, look for the condition. Suffering doesn't automatically teach. Something has to happen for it to.
days.journal: Go back to the thing you wrote on Day 1. What did it teach you? Now write what you would have learned if you'd been humble *before* it hit.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Hebrews 5. Read it one more time. Then read your Day 1 and Day 6 answers.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Why did Jesus have to learn obedience through suffering? And what does that mean for how you learn it?
